# **1\. 	Introduction**  {#1.-introduction}

## **1.1	Project Description**  {#1.1-project-description}

TravelEase is an **accessible travel communication, assistance and institutional improvement system designed for deaf and hard-of-hearing travellers**. The system consists of **a mobile application** for individual travellers and a **web-based dashboard** for tourism and public-service institutions such as airports, hotels, transportation terminals and tourist attractions.

Deaf and hard-of-hearing travellers **may face communication and information barriers** because many travel services depend heavily on spoken communication, public announcements, audible queue numbers and sound-based emergency warnings. For example, travellers may miss a boarding-gate change announced through a loudspeaker, fail to notice that their queue number has been called, experience difficulty communicating with hotel staff or be unable to hear an emergency alarm. These situations can **reduce their independence, affect their ability to complete travel-related activities and create potential safety risks.**

TravelEase addresses these barriers by **converting spoken and audible information into accessible text, visual alerts and vibration notifications**. It also enables deaf users to communicate with people who do not understand sign language through Speech-to-Text, Text-to-Speech, Sign-to-Text and Sign-to-Speech functions. When the communication tools are insufficient, users can send an assistance request directly to the airport, hotel, tourist attraction or transportation facility that they are visiting.

The **institutional dashboard** allows authorised staff to receive assistance requests, communicate with users through text, assign employees and monitor whether the reported problem has been resolved. With the user’s consent, confirmed accessibility problems can also be analysed to identify recurring barriers in particular locations. Institutions can then use the findings to **improve their facilities, staff procedures, visual information systems and accessibility services**.

Therefore, TravelEase **provides both immediate assistance and long-term accessibility improvement**. At the individual level, it helps deaf travellers communicate, receive information and request assistance. At the institutional level, it helps organisations understand where accessibility barriers occur, evaluate their responses and implement appropriate improvements. Its purpose is specifically to improve communication, information accessibility, emergency awareness and institutional support for deaf and hard-of-hearing travellers.

**Modules and Key Functions**

1. User and Institution Management

   The User and Institution Management module **manages the accounts and profiles of both individual users and participating organisations**. Deaf and hard-of-hearing users can register, log in, recover their passwords and manage their personal profiles. They can also configure their preferred languages, communication methods, caption settings, visual-alert preferences, emergency contacts and data-sharing permissions. Institutional users can manage their organisation profiles, branches, service areas, accessibility points, staff accounts and user roles. This module ensures that each user can access the appropriate functions according to their role and communication needs.

2. Location-Based Visual Information and Notifications

   The Location-Based Visual Information and Notifications module **connects users to the correct airport, hotel, tourist attraction or transportation facility**. Users can identify their current institution and area by searching for a location, scanning a QR code or manually selecting a service zone. **After the location has been identified, the system can provide relevant visual announcements**, queue-number notifications, public-announcement captions and emergency alerts. It can also **convert important environmental sounds**, such as alarms, sirens, vehicle horns and door knocking, **into visual, vibration or flash notifications**. Participating institutions can send official textual announcements directly to users in specific areas.

3. Multimodal Accessible Communication

   The **Multimodal Accessible Communication** module serves as the primary real-time conversation engine for deaf and hard-of-hearing travelers, prioritizing computer-vision-based **Sign-to-Text** and **Sign-to-Speech** capabilities. Using the device camera, it tracks active **Malaysian Sign Language** (**BIM**) and **American Sign Language** (**ASL)** gestures, translating physical movements into text strings that travelers can review and edit on a verification screen before the **Sign-to-Speech** engine reads them aloud. In reverse, a **Text-to-Sign** utility maps written phrases back into corresponding sign language visualizations. Building directly upon these sign-based flows, the module integrates a high-resolution **Speech-to-Text (STT)** layer to convert environmental speech from hearing individuals into live captions, alongside a customizable **Text-to-Speech (TTS)** engine to voice typed responses. These tools are unified into a split-screen, real-time two-way dialogue interface featuring multilingual translation, conversation history tracking, phrase shortcuts, and local processing fallbacks for offline communication.  

4. Sign-Language Reference Engine 

   The **Sign-Language Reference Engine** module functions as a specialized, verified visual reference repository designed to support practical travel interactions rather than operating as a comprehensive language education application. It acts as the underlying content provider engine, hosting a curated library of verified **BIM** and **ASL** words and phrases meticulously categorized by specific tourism domains, including airports, hotels, restaurants, transit hubs, tourist attractions, medical facilities, and emergency scenarios. Travelers can programmatically search the directory, bookmark frequently used expressions into a favorites list, and pre-download specific scene packages for reliable offline lookup when network access is unavailable. Each library asset features interactive media components allowing users to view the physical sign gesture, display its corresponding text description, or trigger its matched spoken audio translation. 

5.  Institutional Assistance Request and Response

   The Institutional Assistance Request and Response module allows users to **submit an assistance request to the institution they are currently visiting** when they are unable to obtain information, communicate with staff, locate an accessibility service or understand an emergency instruction. **Institutional staff can receive the request through the dashboard, reply through text, assign an employee and update the request status.** After the institution completes the request, the user can confirm whether the problem was fully resolved, partially resolved or not resolved. Users can also report accessibility barriers that do not require immediate assistance, such as missing visual announcements or sound-only queue systems.

6. SOS and Emergency Communication

   The SOS and Emergency Communication module **supports deaf travellers during urgent or dangerous situations.** Users can activate an SOS request and send a predefined emergency message, their current or last available location and selected emergency information **to an emergency contact**. When the user is inside a participating institution, the request can also be sent **to the institutional dashboard**. The module provides text-based emergency communication, **predefined emergency phrases and an emergency communication card** that explains the user’s preferred communication method. These functions help users obtain assistance when they are unable to hear alarms, spoken evacuation instructions or verbal emergency information.

7. Accessibility Analytics Dashboard and Reporting

   The Accessibility Analytics Dashboard and Reporting module **helps institutions identify recurring accessibility barriers and evaluate their service performance**. The dashboard analyses confirmed accessibility reports, assistance requests, problem locations, problem severity, response times, resolution times, user-confirmed outcomes, repeated requests, announcement delivery and user satisfaction. It can **display accessibility heatmaps, high-frequency problem areas, common issue categories, response performance and satisfaction trends**. The system distinguishes ordinary application usage from confirmed accessibility problems, meaning that simply opening a communication function is not automatically treated as evidence of an institutional barrier. Institutions can **generate monthly, area-specific, problem-category and service-performance reports** to support decisions such as installing visual information screens, improving text-based announcements, revising service procedures or providing staff training.

**Targeted Users**

1. The primary targeted users of TravelEase are **deaf and hard-of-hearing travellers** who **require accessible communication, visual information, environmental alerts or emergency assistance during travel.** These users may have different communication preferences. Some may primarily use sign language, while others may prefer written communication, real-time captions, Text-to-Speech or a combination of visual and vibration-based alerts. TravelEase allows users to select the communication methods that are most suitable for their individual needs.  
2. **Hotel staff and managers** can use TravelEase to support deaf guests during check-in, check-out, facility enquiries, room-related issues, service interruptions and emergency situations. The dashboard can also **help hotel managers identify recurring communication problems**, such as important information being delivered only verbally at the reception counter.  
3. **Airport and transportation management** are also important users of the system. They can **use the institutional dashboard** to send visual travel information, respond to assistance requests, communicate with users through text and provide support for boarding, queueing and emergency situations.  
4. **Tourist-attraction managements** are another targeted group. They can **use the system to review problem patterns, monitor response performance, compare different service areas and plan accessibility improvements**. The reports generated by TravelEase can support decisions concerning staff training, visual information systems, queue notifications, accessible service points and emergency communication procedures.

   

## **1.2	UN SDG and Justification** {#1.2-un-sdg-and-justification}

	\[  \] Goal 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth

	\[/\] Goal 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities

	\[  \] Goal 12: Responsible Consumption and Productions

**Justification:**   
SDG 11 aims to make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable. This goal is the most relevant to TravelEase because **the project focuses on improving the accessibility of transportation facilities, tourism environments and public-facing services for deaf and hard-of-hearing people**.

TravelEase is particularly related to SDG Target 11.2, which promotes safe, accessible and sustainable **transportation systems** for all, with attention to the needs of persons with disabilities. It is also related to SDG Target 11.7, which promotes universal access to safe, inclusive and accessible **public spaces**, particularly for persons with disabilities.

Transportation environments such as airports, railway stations, bus terminals and transit centres **frequently depend on audible announcements and verbal communication**. Passengers may receive information about boarding times, gate changes, delays, cancellations, queue numbers and security instructions through loudspeakers or direct conversation with staff. Deaf and hard-of-hearing travellers may not receive this information at the same time as hearing travellers when a visual alternative is unavailable. TravelEase contributes to accessible transportation by **converting spoken communication and public announcements into text**. It can also **provide official visual updates, queue-number notifications and direct text-based assistance** from transportation staff. For example, when an airport changes a boarding gate, the information can be delivered visually through the TravelEase application. This reduces the user’s dependence on hearing announcements or repeatedly asking other travellers for assistance.

The project also supports more inclusive tourism facilities and public environments. Hotels, restaurants, tourist attractions and visitor-service centres may **rely on verbal communication during check-in, ordering, guided tours, customer service and emergency situations**. TravelEase **provides alternative communication methods** through Speech-to-Text, Text-to-Speech, Sign-to-Text, Sign-to-Speech, visual notifications and Sign languages travel phrases. These functions allow deaf travellers to participate more independently in tourism activities and access services **without always depending on a hearing companion or interpreter**. This supports greater participation by persons with disabilities in transportation, tourism and public life.

TravelEase also contributes to the safety aspect of SDG 11\. Deaf travellers may be **unable to hear alarms, sirens, evacuation announcements or verbal warnings** in public places. The system converts selected environmental sounds and official emergency information into visual, vibration and flash notifications. Users can also **activate an SOS request**, communicate with institutional staff through text and display an emergency communication card. These functions help reduce delays in receiving or responding to important safety information.

Another important contribution is the connection between the individual user and the institution. **Accessibility cannot be achieved only by providing assistive functions on a mobile device.** Airports, hotels, transportation facilities and tourist attractions must also be able to respond to users who require assistance. TravelEase **enables institutions to receive assistance requests**, identify the user’s location and communication preference, assign an employee and monitor whether the issue has been resolved. This makes accessibility support part of the institution’s service process rather than leaving the full responsibility to the traveller.

TravelEase further **supports evidence-based accessibility improvement**. With user consent, **confirmed accessibility problems can be analysed through the institutional dashboard**. Institutions can identify locations with frequent issues, common problem categories, long response times, repeated requests and unresolved accessibility barriers. For example, an airport may discover that deaf travellers frequently report difficulty obtaining boarding information at a particular gate. A hotel may discover that guests repeatedly face communication difficulties at the reception counter because important information is delivered only through speech. 

Overall, **TravelEase contributes to SDG 11 at both the individual and institutional level**s. At the individual level, it provides accessible communication, visual information, environmental awareness and emergency assistance. At the institutional level, it enables airports, hotels, tourist attractions and transportation facilities to respond to users, identify recurring accessibility barriers and evaluate improvement measures. The system therefore **supports the development of cities and tourism environments that are more inclusive, accessible, safe and responsive to the needs of persons with disabilities**.

## **1.3	Background Study** {#1.3-background-study}

Tourism is one of Malaysia's major economic sectors, generating RM291.9 billion and contributing 15.1% to the national economy in 2024 (DOSM, 2025\). As Malaysia continues promoting inclusive and sustainable tourism, ensuring that persons with disabilities can travel independently has become an important national objective. According to the World Health Organization in 2026, more than 430 million people worldwide will experience disabling hearing loss, creating a growing demand for tourism technologies that support accessible communication and equal participation (World Health Organization, 2025\). However, despite the rapid digitalisation of tourism services, many existing travel applications remain primarily designed for hearing users and offer limited accessibility for deaf and hard-of-hearing travellers.

Most current tourism applications focus on travel booking, navigation, itinerary management, and destination recommendations, while communication support is often limited to basic text translation or speech-to-text conversion. Although applications such as Google Translate, Google Live Transcribe, and other speech recognition tools can assist deaf users in specific situations, these solutions are task-specific and require users to switch between multiple applications throughout their journey. More importantly, **they assume that written text is sufficient for communication**. Research has shown that many deaf individuals use sign language as their primary language, whereas written language is learned as a second language. Consequently, **reading complex written information may require greater cognitive effort than for hearing individuals**. Studies by Morford and colleagues suggest that many deaf readers process written English similarly to second-language learners because sign languages possess their own grammar and linguistic structures (A New Reason for Why the Deaf May Have Trouble Reading, 2011\)**.**

These language differences become particularly problematic in tourism environments where **information must often be understood quickly**. Airport announcements, hotel procedures, transportation instructions, emergency notifications, guided tours, and local service interactions are commonly delivered through spoken communication or text-heavy interfaces. While captions and speech-to-text technologies improve accessibility to some extent, **they do not always provide information in the user's most natural language**. Recent Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research further indicates that **Deaf sign-language users generally prefer interfaces that incorporate sign-language videos, intuitive visual layouts, and interactive video elements rather than relying solely on written text**. Accessible video presentation, navigation design, and sign-language-centred interfaces have been shown to **improve usability, comprehension, and user confidence** when interacting with digital systems (Alkhudaidi et al., 2025).

**Several existing systems address individual accessibility needs** of deaf and hard-of-hearing users. Ava similarly provides live captions, Text-to-Speech and multilingual translation (Ava Mobile, n.d.). Hand Talk translates written or spoken content into American Sign Language or Brazilian Sign Language through animated interpreters (Hand Talk, 2026). However, the official descriptions of these systems mainly focus on individual functions such as captioning, sound detection or sign-language presentation. They **do not present a unified tourism-focused platform that combines multilingual communication, sign-language recognition and Sign-to-Speech, location-based travel information, emergency assistance, direct requests to tourism service providers and institutional accessibility analytics.** Their functions are also distributed across separate applications, requiring deaf travellers to use different tools for different situations. Furthermore, Hand Talk currently supports American Sign Language and Brazilian Sign Language rather than Bahasa Isyarat Malaysia. These limitations indicate the need for an integrated platform that supports both the immediate accessibility needs of deaf travellers and the ability of tourism organisations to respond to recurring communication and service barriers.

Consequently, deaf travellers must rely on multiple independent applications, increasing cognitive workload and potentially affecting personal safety during travel. Therefore, there is a clear need for an integrated tourism application specifically designed around the communication preferences and accessibility requirements of deaf and hard-of-hearing users. 

To address this research gap, this project proposes **TravelEase**, an **AI-powered integrated accessibility platform** consisting of a **mobile application** for deaf and hard-of-hearing travellers and a **web-based management dashboard** for tourism service providers. The mobile application combines **real-time multilingual communication, environmental sound detection, emergency assistance, remote safety monitoring, and sign-language learning** within a unified platform to support independent travel. Unlike existing tourism applications that primarily depend on text-based interaction, TravelEase is designed based on accessibility principles and current research on Deaf users' communication preferences. Meanwhile, the web-based dashboard enables organisations such as airports, hotels, hospitals, transportation operators, and tourist attractions to receive assistance requests, monitor accessibility issues, analyse recurring communication barriers, and evaluate the effectiveness of service improvements through data analytics and reporting. By integrating artificial intelligence with accessibility technologies and organisational decision support, TravelEase aims to **improve communication efficiency, enhance traveller safety, support data-driven accessibility improvements, and promote a more inclusive and independent tourism experience**. 

## **1.4	Project Significance** {#1.4-project-significance}

The proposed TravelEase mobile application and enterprise platform significantly **improve the independence and confidence of deaf and hard-of-hearing travellers** by systematically **breaking down communication barriers during transit**. By integrating a dynamic communication module supporting real-time, two-way interactions through speech-to-text, text-to-speech, sign-to-text, and text-to-sign channels, the platform allows users to express themselves fluently and review their conversation history. This core engine is directly supported by a dedicated situational Malaysian Sign Language (BIM) and American Sign Language (ASL) look-up framework, allowing users to quickly pull up verified situational expressions tailored to dynamic travel environments without needing a full learning application. Combined with an intuitive SOS emergency module featuring digitized emergency cards and customizable immediate contacts, the application dramatically **reduces a traveller's constant reliance on external companions or interpreters**, enabling a highly empowering and liberating independent travel experience.

Beyond individual translation utilities, the platform introduces **advanced situational awareness and physical safety layers** through its location and area recognition framework. When travellers navigate major tourism touchpoints; such as airports, hotels, local attractions, or transport facilities; the application automatically identifies the venue to deliver localized push notifications and activate ambient emergency sound detection. This specialized vision and audio translation layer ensures that critical, time-sensitive auditory cues like emergency sirens or flight announcements are instantly converted into highly visible alerts on the user's screen. Furthermore, this structural location recognition automatically pairs the traveller's application with the venue's specific organization dashboard, enabling users to submit direct service requests that on-site staff can instantly claim, manage, and resolve through their backend interface.

The project also provides **substantial long-term benefits to tourism operators and hospitality service providers b**y giving them data-driven tools to enhance operational inclusivity. Through the backend dashboard analytics and reporting engine, the system aggregates anonymized historical data based on the frequency, timing, and types of service requests or accessibility challenges encountered by travelers at specific venues. To **elevate operational management,** the engine integrates staff service completion timings into predictive analytics models, allowing organizations to **forecast potential resource constraints, anticipate peak delay periods, and optimize staff deployment proactively**. Additionally, the platform incorporates a direct traveler feedback feature that allows users to rate their interactions and the quality of assistance provided by individual staff members. By blending these quantitative resolution timelines with qualitative user ratings, organizations like hotel management groups, transit authorities, and local councils can leverage these comprehensive, automatically generated performance reports to audit service quality and strategically prioritize accessibility infrastructure upgrades. This predictive and data-driven capability directly helps businesses optimize staff accountability, elevate customer satisfaction, and **continuously refine overall service protocols,** ensuring that Malaysian hospitality providers can **seamlessly welcome travelers of all physical abilities.** 

Ultimately, TravelEase directly supports the strategic digital transformation goals of the **Visit Malaysia 2026** campaign by building a modern, universally accessible tourism infrastructure. The platform satisfies the rigorous requirements of United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities by leveraging intelligent location-aware safety features, sound detection, and unified communication modules to foster inclusive mobility and universally accessible public services for travelers with disabilities.

# **3\. 	PROJECT FUNCTIONALITIES** {#3.-project-functionalities}

## **3.1	Technology  Stack** {#3.1-technology-stack}

| Category | Technology | Justification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **System Type** | Mobile Application (B2C) & Web-based Dashboard (B2B) | Ensures travelers can access on-the-go communication and safety alerts via smartphones, while providing tourism institutions with a desktop-optimized interface for managing real-time requests and visualizing complex analytical data. |
| **Frontend (Mobile App)** | Flutter | Provides a high-performance, cross-platform mobile application with a responsive and consistent user interface for both Android and iOS deaf travelers using a single codebase. |
| **Frontend (Web Dashboard)** | React.js | Delivers a fast, native web experience for institutional staff. Its extensive ecosystem of UI components and charting libraries (e.g., Chart.js/ECharts) is essential for building professional accessibility heatmaps and analytics dashboards. |
| **Backend & Real-time API** | Supabase (Backend-as-a-Service) | Bridges the Mobile App and Web Dashboard. It provides built-in WebSocket support, enabling instant, real-time push notifications (e.g., SOS or Assistance Requests) from the traveler's phone to the institution's dashboard without page reloads. |
| **Database** | Supabase (PostgreSQL) | Stores user profiles, learning progress, emergency contacts, conversation history, and institutional analytics data in a secure, scalable, cloud-hosted relational database. |
| **AI & Computer Vision** | Python \+ MediaPipe \+ TensorFlow | Supports AI-powered sign language recognition (BIM & ASL) through lightweight hand landmark detection and deep learning models, as well as environmental sound classification for visual alerts. |
| **Speech Recognition** | Google Speech-to-Text API | Converts spoken language into text in real time to facilitate rapid communication between hearing staff/locals and deaf travelers. |
| **Translation Service** | Google Cloud Translation API | Translates text into multiple languages to support seamless communication between users from different linguistic backgrounds. |
| **Maps & Location Services** | Google Maps API | Automatically identifies traveler locations across various tourism venues and supports live location sharing during SOS emergencies. |
